question: What are the three key facts about Canada’s system of government?
options: It is a confederacy, a republic and a commonwealth
It is a monarchy, a theocracy and a union
It is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy
It is a republic, a federation and a direct democracy
explanation: The guide opens its chapter on government with these three facts. Each is then explained in turn.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: our country is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy

question: Which of these is a responsibility of the federal government?
explanation: The federal government handles matters of national and international concern. The other three choices are responsibilities of the provinces.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: These include defence, foreign policy, interprovincial trade and communications, currency, navigation, criminal law and citizenship.
source.license: © Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada, 2021. All rights reserved for commercial reuse

question: Which of these is a responsibility of the provinces?
explanation: The provinces look after matters such as education, health, natural resources and highways. Currency, foreign policy and citizenship are federal.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: The provinces are responsible for municipal government, education, health, natural resources, property and civil rights, and highways.
source.license: © Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada, 2021. All rights reserved for commercial reuse

question: Over which two areas do the federal government and the provinces share jurisdiction?
explanation: Most responsibilities belong to one level of government or the other. Agriculture and immigration are shared between them.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: share jurisdiction over agriculture and immigration
source.license: © Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada, 2021. All rights reserved for commercial reuse

question: In which document were the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments defined in 1867?
options: The British North America Act, now known as the Constitution Act, 1867
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
explanation: Canada is a federal state, with federal, provincial, territorial and municipal governments. The Act of 1867 set out which level is responsible for what.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: the British North America Act, now known as the Constitution Act, 1867

question: What are the three parts of Parliament?
options: The Governor General, the premiers and the mayors
The House of Commons, the Supreme Court and the provinces
The Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the courts
The Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons
explanation: The House of Commons is the representative chamber, elected by the people. Provincial legislatures are made up of the Lieutenant Governor and the elected Assembly.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: Parliament has three parts: the Sovereign (Queen or King), the Senate and the House of Commons.

question: How do senators get their seats?
options: They are chosen by the provincial premiers
They are elected by voters every four years
They are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister
explanation: Senators are appointed, not elected. Members of the House of Commons are the ones elected by the people.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister
source.license: © Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada, 2021. All rights reserved for commercial reuse

question: Until what age do senators serve?
explanation: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister. They serve until they reach 75.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: serve until age 75
source.license: © Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada, 2021. All rights reserved for commercial reuse

question: Who selects the Cabinet ministers?
explanation: In the federal government the Prime Minister chooses the Cabinet. The Prime Minister is also responsible for the operations and policy of the government.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: selects the Cabinet ministers and is responsible for the operations and policy of the government

question: What must happen before a bill can become law in Canada?
options: The Supreme Court must approve it
The provinces must vote on it
The Prime Minister must sign it
Both chambers must pass it and it must receive royal assent
explanation: Both the House of Commons and the Senate consider and review bills. Royal assent is the final step.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: until it has been passed by both chambers and has received royal assent

question: Who grants royal assent to a bill on behalf of the Sovereign?
explanation: No bill can become law until it has received royal assent. The Governor General grants it on behalf of the Sovereign.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: granted by the Governor General on behalf of the Sovereign

question: What must Cabinet ministers do if they are defeated in a non-confidence vote?
options: Nothing: the vote is only advice
Ask the Supreme Court to decide
explanation: Cabinet ministers are responsible to the elected representatives. They must keep the “confidence of the House”.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: have to resign if they are defeated in a non-confidence vote

question: In the legislative process, what happens at the Committee Stage?
options: The bill is printed for the first time
Committee members study the bill clause by clause
explanation: The Committee Stage is the third of seven steps. It comes after second reading, where members debate the principle of the bill.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

question: Who is Canada’s Head of State?
explanation: Canada is a constitutional monarchy. The Sovereign reigns in accordance with the Constitution and is represented in Canada by the Governor General.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: Canada’s Head of State is a hereditary Sovereign (Queen or King)

question: Who is the head of government in Canada?
options: The Speaker of the House of Commons
explanation: The guide draws a clear line between the head of state and the head of government. The Prime Minister actually directs the governing of the country.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: the head of government—the Prime Minister, who actually directs the governing of the country

question: For how long is the Governor General usually appointed?
explanation: The Governor General is appointed by the Sovereign on the advice of the Prime Minister. The appointment is usually for five years.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

question: Who represents the Sovereign in each of the ten provinces?
explanation: The Lieutenant Governor is appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister. The appointment is normally for five years.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: In each of the ten provinces, the Sovereign is represented by the Lieutenant Governor

question: Who represents the federal government in the three territories and plays a ceremonial role?
explanation: Provinces have a Lieutenant Governor, who represents the Sovereign. Territories have a Commissioner instead.

question: What are the three branches of government?
explanation: The three branches work together, and sometimes in creative tension. The guide says this interplay helps to secure the rights and freedoms of Canadians.

explanation: Each province has an elected legislature where provincial laws are passed. The Premier leads the provincial government.

explanation: Municipal governments usually have a council. Its by-laws affect only the local community.

explanation: Municipalities are normally responsible for local services. These include streets and roads, garbage removal, snow removal and firefighting.

question: Who has major responsibilities on First Nations reserves, including housing, schools and other services?
explanation: First Nations have their own leaders. The guide also mentions Aboriginal organizations that speak for First Nations, Métis and Inuit people.

question: Under legislation passed by Parliament, when must federal elections be held?
options: On the first Monday of September every two years
On the third Monday in October every four years following the most recent general election
explanation: This is the fixed date set by legislation. The Prime Minister may ask the Governor General to call an earlier election.

question: What is another name for an electoral district?
explanation: An electoral district is a geographical area represented by a member of Parliament. The citizens of each district elect one MP.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: electoral districts, also known as ridings or constituencies

question: In an electoral district, which candidate becomes the MP?
options: The candidate who receives the most votes
The candidate chosen by the Prime Minister
The candidate chosen by the Governor General
explanation: There can be many candidates in an electoral district. People vote for the candidate and political party of their choice.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: The candidate who receives the most votes becomes the MP for that electoral district.

options: Being at least 18 years old on voting day
explanation: A voter must be a Canadian citizen, at least 18 on voting day, and on the voters’ list. Owning property is not required.

explanation: The lists are produced from the National Register of Electors. Elections Canada also mails a voter information card to each elector once an election is called.

options: No: the list closes a month before
Only if you pay a fee
Yes: you can be added to the voters’ list at any time, including on election day
explanation: The card tells you when and where to vote. A person who did not receive one can still be added to the list.

explanation: The people who run for office are called candidates. There can be many candidates in one electoral district.

question: Your employer insists that you tell them how you voted. What does the guide say?
options: No one has the right to insist that you tell them how you voted
You must tell them if they ask in writing
Only a union representative may ask
explanation: Canadian law secures the right to a secret ballot. You may choose to discuss your vote, but nobody can make you.

question: After an election, who is ordinarily invited by the Governor General to form the government?
options: The leader of the party with the most senators
The premier of the largest province
The leader of the political party with the most seats in the House of Commons
explanation: After being appointed by the Governor General, this leader becomes the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister and the party in power govern as long as they have the confidence of the majority of MPs.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: the leader of the political party with the most seats in the House of Commons

question: What is a minority government?
options: One formed by the smallest party
One with fewer than ten ministers
One where the party in power holds less than half of the seats in the House of Commons
One that has lost an election
explanation: If the party in power holds at least half of the seats, it is a majority government. With fewer than half, it is a minority government.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: If the party in power holds less than half of the seats in the House of Commons, this is called a minority government.

question: What is the opposition party with the most members in the House of Commons called?
explanation: Parties that are not in power are known as opposition parties. Their role is to peacefully oppose or try to improve government proposals.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: The opposition party with the most members of the House of Commons is the Official Opposition

question: What do Cabinet ministers do?
options: They count the ballots after an election
They sit as judges of the Supreme Court
They run the federal government departments
explanation: The Prime Minister chooses the ministers, most of them from among members of the House of Commons. Together they prepare the budget and propose most new laws.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
source.quote_under_25_words: Cabinet ministers are responsible for running the federal government departments.

options: Write the name of the party
Mark an “X” in the circle next to the name of the candidate of your choice
Sign your name beside the candidate
explanation: You go behind a screen to mark the ballot, because the vote is secret. Then you fold it and present it to the poll officials.

source.quote_under_25_words: Mark an “X” in the circle next to the name of the candidate of your choice.

Vote at the advance polls or by special ballot
explanation: The dates and location of the advance polls are on the voter information card. A special ballot is the other choice.

question: What does the presumption of innocence mean?
options: Everyone is innocent until proven guilty
The police decide who is guilty
Everyone is guilty until proven innocent
explanation: The Canadian justice system guarantees everyone due process under the law. The presumption of innocence applies in criminal matters.

source.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

question: What is due process?
options: The right to a second trial
The time allowed to pay a fine
The principle that the government must respect all the legal rights a person is entitled to under the law
explanation: Due process is part of the heritage on which Canada’s legal system is based. That heritage also includes the rule of law and freedom under the law.

explanation: Canada is governed by an organized system of laws. Nobody is outside them, whatever office they hold.
